▸WHAT THE LAW HERE COUNTS AS ENGINEERED
Technique-basedwith a carve-out
Regulation attaches to the technique. If a laboratory method was used the organism goes through the biosafety system, however small the change and whether or not the same result could have come from ordinary breeding. This is the strictest of the three, and the one the industry lobbies hardest against, because a one-letter edit is treated the same as inserting a gene from another species. It is also the only approach under which gene-edited organisms reliably stay visible: they are assessed, they get a record, and there is a window in which the public can comment before a decision.
▸THE CARVE-OUT
At least one whole class of engineered organism has been put outside registration, usually organisms edited without inserting DNA from another species. They are not assessed, not notified, not tracked and in most places not labelled: the law simply never reaches them, so there is no file to ask for and no comment window. This is the fastest-growing approach in the world, and it makes objecting pointless rather than difficult. There is no permit to oppose, no deadline to meet, and a group that has learned to fight applications finds there are no applications left to fight.
Everything the exemption does not reach — a plant carrying a gene from another species, for instance — still goes through the scheme above, and is assessed, recorded and open to comment in the ordinary way.
▸DECISIONS FILED TO THE CARTAGENA PROTOCOL
72 decisions filed by this country. A decision is a ruling on whether a living modified organism may be used, imported or released here.

act:
What you can do about this
▸TEST IT YOURSELF6
NARO / prefectural laboratories
TESTING
The national agriculture research organisation runs GMO detection and publishes the official methods.
Visit source ↗
EnviroLogix QuickStix
TESTING
Lateral flow strips, the same format as a pregnancy test. Crush tissue or seed in water, dip, read in five to ten minutes. Sold to anyone, a few pounds each, in packs. Strips are trait-specific, so know which trait to look for before buying.
Visit source ↗
Romer Labs AgraStrip
TESTING
Strips plus the extraction kits that go with them, sold internationally — which matters because the trait to test for differs by region.
Visit source ↗
Agdia ImmunoStrip
TESTING
Sells in small quantities with published prices, which makes it the most usable of the three for someone testing a handful of samples rather than a lorry.
Visit source ↗
Eurofins — laboratory GMO testing
TESTING
The largest food and feed testing network in the world, with laboratories in more than 60 countries and the default commercial route for a confirmatory DNA test. A strip result tells you what to do next; this is what an enforcement body acts on.
Visit source ↗
GMOMETHODS — the EU database of validated detection methods, and the ENGL laboratory network
IF YOU ARE COMMISSIONING A TEST, THIS IS WHERE THE METHOD COMES FROM. An application to authorise a GM food or feed in the EU MUST INCLUDE A METHOD FOR DETECTING, IDENTIFYING AND QUANTIFYING IT, and the EU Reference Laboratory (EURL GMFF, hosted by the Joint Research Centre) validates that method for sensitivity, specificity, accuracy and reliability. The validated methods are then PUBLISHED FREE in the GMOMETHODS database, searchable by EVENT, UNIQUE IDENTIFIER, SPECIES, APPLICANT and technique. So for most authorised events anywhere in the world there is a published, peer-validated PCR method a laboratory can be asked to run — and the unique identifier this map keeps telling readers to write down is the key to finding it. The JRC also publishes decision tools, GMO-MATRIX and EVENT-FINDER. Behind it sits the EUROPEAN NETWORK OF GMO LABORATORIES (ENGL), the national enforcement laboratories of every EU country PLUS NORWAY, SWITZERLAND AND TURKEY. THE HONEST LIMIT: detecting UNAUTHORISED GMOs relies on screening that only indicates presence and needs confirmation by other approaches; and the EURL and ENGL's own report of 26 March 2019 addresses the difficulty of detecting organisms made by NEW MUTAGENESIS TECHNIQUES — gene-edited plants may leave nothing a method can target. Work on GM animals and microorganisms is still in progress.
Visit source ↗
▸WHO AUTHORISES A RELEASE4
MAFF — Cartagena Law
REGULATOR
Authorises agricultural releases.
Visit source ↗
Ministry of the Environment
REGULATOR
Shares responsibility for environmental release.
Visit source ↗
Biosafety Clearing-House — national focal points
REGULATOR
Every party to the Cartagena Protocol must name a contact for biosafety, and the list is public. For most of the world it is the only named biosafety contact that exists, and it holds the decisions filed for that country.
Visit source ↗
Biosafety Clearing-House — what a country profile holds
Referenced by 135 rows in this box. A country profile on the Clearing-House holds the national focal point and competent authorities the country has notified, its national biosafety law where filed, and the decisions it has submitted under Article 20. It is a country's OWN FILINGS, so a thin profile means the country has filed little — not that it decides little. Filing is a treaty obligation without a sanction for missing it.
Visit source ↗
▸WHO TAKES A COMPLAINT7
Prefectural ordinances and guidelines on open-air GM cultivation (Japan)
COMPLAINT
Japan's prefectures inspect and enforce; the ministries authorise. A complaint about a site or a crop goes to the prefecture. THIS IS THE LAYER TO USE IN JAPAN. At least TEN OF THE 47 PREFECTURES have their own ordinances or guidelines on OPEN-AIR CULTIVATION of GM plants, explicitly to prevent cross-pollination with related crops in the region — among them HOKKAIDO, NIIGATA, CHIBA, KYOTO, IBARAKI, SHIGA, IWATE, HYOGO and TOKYO, with municipal guidelines spreading too (Tsukuba). THE NUMBERS ARE THE POINT: Hokkaido sets minimum isolation distances of AT LEAST 300 METRES FOR RICE, 1.2 KM FOR CORN AND 2 KM FOR SUGAR BEET — about TWICE the distances the agriculture ministry sets for its own research entities. Niigata's ordinance OBLIGES FARMERS TO OBTAIN PERMISSION to grow GM crops and requires research institutes to FILE REPORTS on open-air experiments, with penalties for violation. For anyone seeking a workable separation distance or a local permission regime, these are drafted, adopted and in force. Nationally, MAFF, the Ministry of the Environment and NIES run an ANNUAL SURVEY of escaped imported GM canola and soy AROUND MAJOR PORTS AND ROADS under the Cartagena Act — published monitoring of volunteer GM plants, reported to the Cartagena Protocol meetings.
Visit source ↗
Consumer Affairs Agency (消費者庁) — food labelling
COMPLAINT
Japan requires labelling of specified engineered foods, and this is the body that takes a complaint about one. Japan is a large importer and a very small grower, so labelling is where most disputes here actually arise. Japan labels specified engineered foods; this is where a complaint about one goes. What is actually labelled, and what changed on 1 April 2023: mandatory GM labelling covers nine agricultural products — soybeans, corn, potatoes, rapeseed, cottonseed, alfalfa, sugar beet, papaya and mustard greens — and processed foods made from them WHERE THE MODIFIED DNA OR PROTEIN IS STILL DETECTABLE after processing, monitored across 33 product categories. The voluntary side tightened: previously a product with up to 5% unintentional presence could be called 'not genetically modified'; since April 2023 only 'not detected' may carry that claim, and 5% or less is labelled as separately managed in production and sale. High-oleic soybeans were dropped from mandatory labelling because the trait can be produced by conventional breeding — the same detectability logic that puts gene-edited products outside labelling in several countries on this map.
Visit source ↗
The Cartagena focal point, when nothing else is named
Every party to the Cartagena Protocol names a national focal point, and the Clearing-House publishes the current office. Where this map does not name the body that takes a complaint in a country, that office is the one obliged to answer a question about a living modified organism, and it can say which national authority handles the rest. It is the fallback of last resort rather than the right first stop: a focal point is a correspondence address, not an inspectorate.
Visit source ↗
IPPC national plant protection organisation contacts
Every IPPC contracting party maintains a national plant protection organisation, and its contact details are published country by country. This is the body that handles a plant pest or a quarantine question, and in most countries it is also the body with inspectors who can actually enter a field. Animal research is self-regulated through institutional committees under national guidelines; there is no licensing authority and no register of establishments. The structure is deliberate and stated as such. After the education and health ministries each issued basic policies on animal experiments in institutions, they asked the Science Council of Japan to write model guidelines each institution could build its own rules from — published 2006. The Council's own text argues that self-management outside legislation is sometimes called the North American model and that Japan should build a system rooted in its own ground. Most countries license animal research through an agriculture, health or home affairs ministry and inspect on a schedule. Whether the public may complain, and whether reports are published, varies enormously — the two questions worth asking first.
The Animal Welfare Body inside the institution, and the WOAH animal welfare focal point
Two routes exist almost everywhere even where no public register does. FIRST, INSIDE THE INSTITUTION. Under EU DIRECTIVE 2010/63/EU — followed closely in Switzerland, the UK and Norway too — every authorised establishment MUST HAVE AN ANIMAL WELFARE BODY, comprising at least one person with practical knowledge of animal care and husbandry, ONE SCIENTIFIC MEMBER, AND A DESIGNATED VETERINARIAN. It advises on acquisition, care, housing and use, applies the 3Rs, KEEPS TRACK OF HOW PROJECTS AFFECT THE ANIMALS, and advises on project applications — so an internal record exists of what is being done and at what severity, and a NON-TECHNICAL PROJECT SUMMARY is published for each authorised project. National competent authorities grant authorisation and INSPECT breeders, suppliers and research establishments, and each Member State has a NATIONAL COMMITTEE for the protection of animals used for scientific purposes. SECOND, INTERNATIONALLY. Each of WOAH's 182 member countries nominates a NATIONAL FOCAL POINT FOR ANIMAL WELFARE, alongside focal points for veterinary laboratories and wildlife. Where no national body is named in this box, that focal point is a real named official who can be asked who licenses and who inspects. Note WOAH's animal welfare standards, unlike its health standards, DO NOT FALL UNDER THE WTO SPS AGREEMENT, so they carry no trade enforcement.

▸WHAT IS PUBLISHED, AND WHAT IS NOT1
Where the numbers come from, and what they leave out — CCAC, the UK count, and the countries with none
ONLY A HANDFUL OF COUNTRIES COUNT AT ALL, and each counts something different — which is why global totals in this field should be read as estimates. BRITAIN counts every regulated procedure on a protected animal under the ANIMALS (SCIENTIFIC PROCEDURES) ACT 1986, covering all vertebrates AND CEPHALOPODS, published annually by the Home Office, with NORTHERN IRELAND counting separately. THE EXCLUSIONS ARE THE POINT. Canada's CCAC covers only CERTIFIED INSTITUTIONS — typically universities — so most private laboratories and companies are absent unless government-funded, and the CCAC sets no standardised submission method. The US counts only AWA-covered mammals, excluding mice, rats and birds; official figures near 800,000 sit against unofficial estimates of 12–24 million. INVERTEBRATES SUCH AS FRUIT FLIES AND WORMS ARE NOT PROTECTED AND NOT COUNTED ANYWHERE. And JAPAN PUBLISHES NO OFFICIAL GOVERNMENT DATA at all — the only figures come from a professional association survey to which a third of facilities did not respond. Where a country publishes nothing, an estimate is all that exists.

▸WHO OVERSEES CONTAINMENT3
MEXT — Cartagena Law contained use

Contained use is approved by the education and science ministry; approvals are not published facility by facility. Japan's Cartagena Law splits use in two. Type 1 use is use WITHOUT containment measures, and requires the user to set out a usage plan and obtain ministerial approval in advance. Type 2 use is use WITH containment — laboratory work, storage and transport — and here containment must be applied to every recombinant experiment regardless of level; where the ministerial ordinance does not prescribe the measures for a given case, the minister's confirmation must be obtained each time. Six ministries share the implementing rules. Organisms produced by genome editing are assessed against whether they fall within the law's definition of a living modified organism, which is where the boundary is drawn.

In most countries laboratory work is notified rather than licensed, notifications are not published, and there is no public complaint route. The honest first question is which body holds the notifications — ask the Cartagena focal point.

In most countries contained laboratory work is NOTIFIED rather than licensed and no public register is created — which is why 184 of the country boxes in this file carry no national entry here. A second tier usually does exist. Under the CARTAGENA PROTOCOL, LMOs destined for CONTAINED USE fall under ARTICLE 6 and are EXEMPT FROM THE ADVANCE INFORMED AGREEMENT PROCEDURE — contained work is deliberately outside the route that generates public records — though the handling and labelling duties in Article 18 still apply and a Party MAY REQUIRE NOTIFICATION BEFORE TRANSIT. What national biosafety frameworks create instead is an INSTITUTIONAL BIOSAFETY COMMITTEE inside every organisation doing the work, usually with a named BIOSAFETY OFFICER and PRINCIPAL INVESTIGATOR, CERTIFIED BY AND REPORTING TO the national biosafety committee. Ghana's Biosafety (Management of Biotechnology) Regulations 2007 set this out explicitly, as do India's Rules 1989. THE PRACTICAL POINT: where no national register exists, the record of what a laboratory is doing sits with that institution's own biosafety committee, and the national focal point listed on the Biosafety Clearing-House is who can be asked whether one has been certified.
